content: Functional daytime urinary incontinence in children refers to the involuntary leakage of urine while the child is awake. The normal development of bladder control progresses during early childhood, with daytime continence typically achieved before nighttime continence. By the age of five, most children have developed sufficient control over daytime urination, including the ability to appropriately delay voiding. Neurological or physical causes, such as congenital abnormalities or urinary tract infections, are often identified in children with daytime wetting and should be thoroughly investigated first. If these causes are excluded, further underlying factors may be challenging to determine, and treatment is often guided by the classification of the condition. The International Children's Continence Society (ICCS) has proposed a classification system for functional incontinence, which considers the two primary functions of the bladder: storage and voiding. Urine storage is a continuous process as the kidneys drain into the bladder, leading to a sensation of fullness at a specific threshold. Voluntary control by the brain's cortical centers allows for urination, which involves contraction of the bladder muscle (detrusor) and simultaneous relaxation of the pelvic floor muscles and urinary sphincters. Children are expected to void between 65% and 150% of their expected bladder capacity, which can be calculated as the child’s age in years plus one, multiplied by 30 milliliters. The ICCS classification includes various subtypes of incontinence, such as urgency incontinence (overactive bladder), underactive bladder, voiding postponement, dysfunctional voiding (bladder-sphincter dyssynergia), bladder outlet obstruction, stress incontinence, giggle incontinence (enuresis risoria), vaginal reflux, daytime urinary frequency, and bladder neck dysfunction. Daytime urinary incontinence is difficult to quantify due to differences in interpretation and classification. Studies estimate that approximately 17% of school-aged children experience daytime incontinence. The prevalence decreases with age, with children aged seven experiencing incontinence episodes at a rate of 6.3% to 9% per month, compared to 1.1% to 4.2% in children aged 11 to 13 years. Daytime incontinence episodes are more common in girls than boys as they grow older, with rates of 3.6% to 4.7% in girls aged 15 to 17 years compared to 0.3% to 0.9% in boys of the same age. Children with daytime incontinence often also experience nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting), although the underlying mechanisms of these conditions are thought to differ. Daytime urinary incontinence significantly impacts a child’s psychosocial development, contributing to behavioral problems, poor academic performance, and reduced school engagement. It also negatively affects both child-reported and parent-reported quality of life, with a greater impact than nocturnal enuresis. While there are no published estimates of the direct costs of urinary incontinence in children, studies in adults suggest that pharmaceutical management of incontinence can reduce activity impairment and improve quality of life. Treatment strategies for functional daytime incontinence include urotherapy, which involves regulating fluid intake, managing constipation, timed voiding, and optimizing voiding posture. Urotherapy forms the foundation of all treatment approaches and should be tailored to the child based on clinical history, bladder diaries, non-invasive urodynamic studies, and response to therapy. For children with voiding-phase issues, alpha-adrenergic receptor antagonists (alpha blockers) may be prescribed. These medications are particularly useful in cases of bladder neck dysfunction, dysfunctional voiding, idiopathic urinary retention, or when other conventional therapies have failed. Alpha blockers used in children with functional daytime urinary incontinence include non-selective agents (e.g., phenoxybenzamine, phentolamine, tolazoline, trazodone) that act on both α1 and α2 receptors, and selective α1 blockers (e.g., alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, tamsulosin, terazosin, silodosin). Selective α2 blockers (e.g., atipamezole, idazoxan, mirtazapine, yohimbine) have not been used for bladder treatment, and the role of α2 receptors in humans remains unclear. The cost of alpha blockers for children is not well-documented, but studies in other contexts suggest they are relatively inexpensive, at approximately $2 per pill. Alpha blockers work by relaxing the smooth muscle in the bladder neck and urethra, facilitating urine flow and improving voiding efficiency. Some non-selective and selective alpha blockers also act on the detrusor muscle via alpha-1D receptors, mimicking the effects of anticholinergic medications. This action reduces bladder overactivity, urgency, and involuntary contractions, thereby improving symptoms. Compared to other treatments, alpha blockers have minimal side effects, with postural hypotension (lightheadedness or dizziness upon standing) being the most common in non-selective agents. In contrast, anticholinergic medications, which are frequently used for daytime incontinence, have a higher side-effect profile that often leads to discontinuation. Surgical interventions, such as botulinum toxin A injections, also carry risks of adverse effects. Daytime urinary incontinence is a stigmatizing condition that affects a child’s daily activities, social interactions, and educational experiences. Effective treatment can significantly improve a child’s psychosocial development and quality of life. If left untreated, symptoms may persist into adulthood. As our understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying different subtypes of functional daytime incontinence evolves, it is clear that pharmacological interventions must be tailored to the individual. Alpha blockers are currently used variably and often as a last resort due to limited data on their efficacy in children. A comprehensive review of the use of alpha blockers for functional daytime urinary incontinence in children is therefore necessary to guide clinical practice and optimize treatment outcomes.
